body:
Yes. This is a very annoying and strange behaviour.
This is a stripped code from my last game.
```gdscript
var attack_player
attack_player = func (node: Node3D):
	if node is Player:
		# more code...
		attack_area.body_entered.disconnect(attack_player)
attack_area.body_entered.connect(attack_player)
```
```
Invalid type in function 'disconnect' in base 'Signal'. Cannot convert argument 1 from Nil to Callable.
```
You can get around this strange behaviour by declaring your Callable inside the script scope.
```gdscript
extends FSMState

var attack_player: Callable

func _do_stuff():
	attack_player = func (node: Node3D):
		if node is Player:
			# more code...
			attack_area.body_entered.disconnect(attack_player)
			# ^ this will work
	attack_area.body_entered.connect(attack_player)
````

A local lambda can't refer to itself during its initialization since it doesn't have a name yet. It doesn't work in other languages too.
Most languages would give a parser error rather than a runtime error, though.

The key issue here is the fact that GDScript's lambda function only copies value of the captured variables rather than the reference of them, [as mentioned in the documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/scripting/gdscript/gdscript_basics.html#lambda-functions), and there isn't a particular straight-forward way for achieving references without a dedicated array of RCed type.

This is expected (though not obvious) behavior. Lambdas capture local variables by value (making copies) when the lambda is created. This is described in the [documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/scripting/gdscript/gdscript_basics.html#lambda-functions). See also https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/8558 for a more detailed example. Changing this behavior is not possible due to the memory management model. GDScript does not have a garbage collector, and lambdas can outlive captured local variables, which should be destroyed when the function ends.

Perhaps we should add a warning if a lambda captures a local variable that it is assigned to upon creation (although more complex cases are possible here, for example, if the lambda is stored in an array). The warning message should indicate that the old value will be captured. This is similar to the existing `CONFUSABLE_CAPTURE_REASSIGNMENT` warning.

Lambdas have the ability to provide an optional function name:

```gdscript
var callable: Callable = func my_lambda() -> void:
    print("test")
```

Currently, this is only used for debugging, but it might make sense to allow this name to be used for recursive calls.

As a workaround, you can pass the lambda itself as a parameter:

```gdscript
var recursive_countdown: Callable = func (self_callable: Callable, number: int) -> void:
    if number <= 0:
        return
    print(number)
    self_callable.call(self_callable, number - 1)
recursive_countdown.call(recursive_countdown, 3)
```

* See also https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/8857.

This makes me thinking about introducing a dedicated generic RefCounted cell (aka Array with only one element) for this specific use case, e.g.:
```gdscript
var recursive_countdown: Rc[Callable];
recursive_countdown.value = func (number: int) -> void:
    if number <= 0:
        return
    print(number)
    recursive_countdown.value.call(number - 1)
recursive_countdown.value.call(3)
```
~~definitely not inspired by rust~~

> This makes me thinking about introducing a dedicated generic RefCounted cell (aka Array with only one element) for this specific use case

For this specific case (recursive lambdas), I would prefer to be able to access the lambda inside itself using an optional function name or "nested" functions (implicit lambdas).

A generic `RefCounted` container (`Rc[T]`, `Boxed[T]`, etc.) might be useful for other purposes (for example, to simulate passing value types by reference). But to me it seems unjustified given the lack of a unified type system and the scope of the required changes (there are no generic object types in core, and typed arrays/dictionaries take up a lot of code in the GDScript analyzer).

As you mentioned, you can currently use (typed) arrays of size 1 as a workaround. This trick is even used in the engine API.

---

The ability to use an optional function name inside the lambda seems like a relatively simple change, with almost no impact on the language design:

```gdscript
var recursive_countdown: Callable = func recursive_countdown(number: int) -> void:
    if number <= 0:
        return
    print(number)
    recursive_countdown.call(number - 1) # Or `recursive_countdown(number - 1)`?
recursive_countdown.call(3)
```

"Nested" functions (implicit lambdas) look good at first glance, but have the disadvantage of hiding the fact that the lambda is created at the time of use, which is already not very obvious to users and often causes confusion.

```gdscript
func recursive_countdown(number: int) -> void:
    if number <= 0:
        return
    print(number)
    recursive_countdown(number - 1)
recursive_countdown.call(3)
```

> The ability to use an optional function name inside the lambda seems like a relatively simple change, with almost no impact on the language design

Unfortunately, I've somewhat exaggerated the simplicity of this change. It's feasible, but it likely requires a compatibility break and has a couple of caveats.

First, the lambda function name is currently not involved in name resolution at all. You can "shadow" it with a local variable or constant:

```gdscript
var callable: Callable = func my_func() -> void:
    var my_func: int = 123
    print(my_func)
callable.call()
```

Second, we need to consider not only the current lambda, but also the parent ones:

```gdscript
var f = func (x):
    var g = func (y):
        if y <= 0:
            if x > 0:
                f.call(x - 1) # <-- !!!
            return
        prints(x, y)
        g.call(y - 1)
    g.call(x)
f.call(3)
```

I think it might be worth to just add some more clear checks to warn in this case and suggest using alternative ways of solving it, considering the cost of permitting it and the potential foot-gun of allowing it generally (granted all recursion is a potential foot-gun, but depends on the case how easy it is to cause accidentally), if a workaround is trivial

IMHO the only real problem here is that displayed error message is cryptic for unaware users ; thus simply explaing limitation in an error message providing link to documentation with additionnal workaround example would be nice,  I agree with AThousandShips.
